title: IT Threat Intel - IT Cybersecurity
description: Curated IT / enterprise cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_threatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Microsoft has taken down EvilTokens, a phishing service that compromised more than 12,000 Microsoft accounts at over 10,000 organisations — MFA did not stop it, because victims completed the sign-in themselves
items.content_text: Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, working with Health-ISAC, law enforcement and SpyCloud, disrupted the EvilTokens phishing-as-a-service platform on 22 September. Microsoft tracks the operators as Storm-2992. Since February 2026 the service had compromised more than 12,000 Microsoft accounts at more than 10,000 organisations in 79 countries; SpyCloud separately verified 8,708 compromised accounts across 6,585 corporate domains, and 97.5% of victims were on enterprise domains. The United States was hit hardest, followed by Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia. Named sectors are wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education and healthcare. The technique needs no stolen password and no fake login page. EvilTokens abused Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth 2.0 device-authorization flow: the victim is sent a code and asked to enter it on a genuine Microsoft page, and by completing that sign-in, MFA included, they hand the attacker’s session a valid token. Subscribers paid US$500 a month or US$1,500 once, and the kit included AI features to write lures and sift compromised mailboxes for high-value targets. The Metropolitan Police arrested two men, aged 32 and 38, at addresses in Canary Wharf and Nine Elms; both are on bail. This leads the edition because it is the widest confirmed compromise on the page, across every sector, and because the disruption does not close the hole: a successor service, APToken, has already appeared, and tokens already issued to attackers can keep working until they are revoked. Four exploited edge and management flaws added to KEV on 22 September (Check Point twice, F5 and Arista) sit below it in Critical Advisories. They are serious, but each is a discrete patch-and-hunt job.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit; SpyCloud; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Active from Feb 2026; disrupted 22 Sep 2026

items.title: ShinyHunters defaced the FBI’s jobs portal and claims a PeopleSoft zero-day — the defacement and the investigation are confirmed, the zero-day and the terabytes are only claimed
items.content_text: The FBIJobs.gov applicant portal went offline after a subdomain was defaced with ShinyHunters branding reading “This site has been seized by ShinyHunters” on the night of 21 September. The FBI told Cybersecurity Dive that “while the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third-party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating”, and that it is working with the third-party providers that support the portal. 404 Media reviewed a sample the group supplied and found that some of it matched real personnel data. Those are the confirmed facts. The rest is ShinyHunters’ claim: that it got in through a zero-day in Oracle PeopleSoft, the HR platform; that it took data on “almost ALL FBI Agents” and job applicants, 2–3 TB in total; that it reached Criminal Justice, HR and “Medlink” systems and FBI-managed AWS GovCloud; and that it is now using the same bug against Fortune 500 companies. Oracle declined to comment, and no CVE has been confirmed by Oracle; this card does not cite one. The group says it acted in retaliation for a May FBI bulletin about it and wants that bulletin corrected or removed. It is the same group that hijacked Clop’s leak site this month (see that card). For everyone else the practical question is PeopleSoft: if the zero-day is real, internet-facing PeopleSoft HR and Campus Solutions deployments are the exposure.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI statement via Cybersecurity Dive; BleepingComputer; 404 Media; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Defacement 21 Sep 2026; reported 22 Sep 2026; FBI update 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Brevo’s own embedded scripts were rewritten at the CDN edge to serve ClickFix lures and a WordPress backdoor — Sansec estimates more than 100,000 sites were exposed
items.content_text: Email-marketing platform Brevo, formerly Sendinblue, has confirmed a two-stage compromise that ended with its own customer-embedded scripts serving malware. On 14 September, between about 16:07 and 20:30 UTC, attackers used a long-lived Cloudflare API key with full account permissions that had been hardcoded in Brevo’s application source code to deploy a Cloudflare Worker that rewrote responses at the CDN edge. The Worker altered brevo.com, sendinblue.com, the login and account hosts and sibforms.com form hosting. It also altered the forms, Conversations chat widget and SDK loader scripts that customers embed in their own sites, and it stripped Content-Security-Policy headers along the way. Ordinary visitors to those sites were shown a fake “Cloudflare, verify you are human” ClickFix page telling them to paste and run a command. For visitors logged in as WordPress administrators, the script tried to install a malicious plugin, “Web Media Optimizer”, as a persistent backdoor with a hardcoded authentication bypass. Sansec, which first reported the attack, estimates that more than 100,000 websites were likely exposed; Brevo has not published its own count. Brevo says the key was first misused in late August, but it found no injection into customer-facing pages before 14 September. Its origin servers were never modified, and because the change happened at the edge, “standard integrity checks did not detect the change”. The first stage, on 10 September, was separate. An improperly scoped SAML single sign-on path gave the attacker access to 138 Brevo customer accounts; contacts were exported from 43 of them and phishing was sent from six. It reached every organisation that pasted the vendor’s script tag into its site: retailers, charities, schools and law firms alike. Sansec’s write-up, last revised on 17 September, puts the exposure at 100,000 or more sites; Brevo has not published a customer count. The story led the previous two editions and moves here now that it is contained and a wider confirmed campaign has taken the lead. Brevo has revoked the key, removed the hardcoded credentials, deleted the attacker’s hostnames and purged its edge caches. It cannot clean the WordPress sites that received the plugin, or the computers of visitors who ran the command.

_threatfeed.source_name: Brevo incident write-up; Sansec; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Injection 14 Sep 2026; disclosed 16–17 Sep 2026

items.title: Canva confirms that a breach at its feedback vendor Canny reached its Salesforce account — Canva calls it limited business-contact and contract data, and the attackers’ far larger claims are unverified
items.content_text: Canva has confirmed that “the unauthorised access to Canny allowed access to limited enterprise customer information through its connection to our Salesforce account, including business contact details and contract information.” Canny, a product-feedback vendor, was hit on 28 August and notified Canva on the 29th. A new group calling itself “The Seven Deadly Sins” claims much more: over 2 million CRM records and 200 million data-warehouse rows from Canva, 3.8 TB in total, and access to more than 300 Jira instances and 50-plus Salesforce, HubSpot and Zendesk tenants at other companies, naming Mercury.com and Proxyscrape.io. None of that is confirmed, and Canva did not respond to DataBreaches.net about the wider claims. The confirmed part is the useful one. Nobody broke into Canva’s own platform. A small vendor holding a connection into Canva’s CRM was breached, and that connection carried the data out. It is the same path as the Salesloft Drift and Gainsight incidents of 2025, and every connected app in your CRM is another one.

_threatfeed.source_name: Canva statement via DataBreaches.net
_threatfeed.date_note: Canny intrusion 28 Aug 2026; public 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Elsevier’s nursing and drug-reference platforms redirected users and API sign-ins to LAPSUS$-branded extortion pages — Elsevier confirms the redirect and calls it narrowly scoped
items.content_text: On 21 September visitors to several Elsevier platforms were redirected to extortion pages on lapsus[.]ar[.]io and lapsus[.]bz. The affected platforms were Evolve and Sherpath, used by nursing and health-science programmes, ClinicalPharmacology, and the Gold Standard Drug Database (GSDD) APIs. Token requests to api.gsdd.net/auth/AccessToken were redirected too. Elsevier confirms that “visitors to select platforms were being redirected to a third-party page”, says the issue is resolved and service restored, and describes a “narrowly scoped, limited-duration event” with no indication that core platforms or customer data were compromised. The incident was first reported by Sorami Consulting and covered by DataBreaches.net, which reported that nursing students were locked out of exams and simulated charting. “LAPSUS$” is the name on the redirect domains. No investigator has attributed the incident to the original group. The broader point is the API redirect. Clinical and campus systems that call drug-reference or courseware APIs sent their authentication requests to an attacker’s page, so any client that followed the redirect and sent credentials should be treated as having leaked them.

_threatfeed.source_name: Elsevier statement via DataBreaches.net; Sorami Consulting
_threatfeed.date_note: Redirects 21 Sep 2026; reported 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Researchers report an operator using open-source AI agent frameworks to plant card skimmers on more than 100 sites and collect over 600,000 card records — a single vendor’s findings, no victim named
items.content_text: Security start-up Gambit reported on 23 September that a financially motivated, apparently Chinese-speaking operator ran a card-skimming campaign from July to 22 September using three open-source agent frameworks: Strix for discovery, Cairn for exploitation and an orchestration layer called Hermes, which Gambit says was configured to use Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 model. Gambit counts skimmers on more than 100 sites (119 in its data), at least 27 companies breached, and more than 600,000 card records. Magento databases were among the targets. Injection points included edited JavaScript files, script tags on checkout pages, Google Tag blocks, poisoned S3, CDN and server caches, database fields, Kubernetes deployments and cron jobs. Unnamed victims include a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, an industrial distributor and an online fashion retailer, and Gambit puts the operator’s cost at about US$25 per target. All figures come from one vendor and no victim has confirmed. The report describes an attacker misusing open-source tooling. It does not say the model provider’s platform was compromised. The techniques themselves are old. The report’s claim is that agents let one operator run them against dozens of targets at once.

_threatfeed.source_name: Gambit research via BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign July–22 Sep 2026; reported 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Gyazo lost 23.6 million user records and 490 million image-metadata records through its upload server — including session IDs, X integration tokens and text read from users’ screenshots
items.content_text: Helpfeel, the Japanese company behind the screenshot-sharing service Gyazo, has disclosed that an attacker exploited a flaw in its image upload server on 11 September and was removed on the 12th. The attacker took about 23.62 million user records, including anonymous accounts with no email address, plus about 490 million image-metadata records and a list of private images. The user fields include names or nicknames, email addresses, password hashes, user and device IDs, login session IDs, X (Twitter) integration tokens, Google sign-in emails and subscription status. The image metadata includes upload IP addresses, user agents, EXIF location data, titles, hashed passphrases and text extracted from screenshots by OCR. Payment card data was not affected. Helpfeel says it is still working out how many individuals are affected; it took the service offline, fixed the flaw, contacted the authorities and notified users. For an enterprise, the OCR text is a bigger concern than the account data. Screenshot tools tend to be installed informally, and people use them to capture dashboards, error messages, configuration pages and chat threads. Any credential, internal hostname or customer detail that appeared in a Gyazo screenshot may now sit as searchable text in the attacker’s copy. Update, 21 September: Infosecurity Magazine reports that Helpfeel’s 16 September notice says the exposed metadata could let a third party view the corresponding images without authorisation, and that the company has temporarily disabled viewing of some images; researcher Damian Skeeles notes the dataset relates to images registered in January 2019 or earlier. The headline figures are unchanged.

_threatfeed.source_name: Helpfeel notice; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 11 Sep 2026; disclosed 16 Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026; follow-up 21 Sep 2026

items.title: A May npm-worm infection on a developer’s machine surfaced in September as a public leak of CrowdSec’s private repositories
items.content_text: CrowdSec, the open-source intrusion-prevention company, has traced a leak of its private source code back to the TanStack npm compromise of 11 May 2026. In that attack, TeamPCP pushed 84 malicious versions across 42 packages (CVE-2026-45321) carrying the “Shai-Hulud” credential-harvesting malware. The machine of a departed CrowdSec developer was infected, which exposed a GitHub OAuth token. On 22 May, in nine minutes between 05:52 and 06:01 UTC, about 170 private repositories were downloaded. The access was removed on 25 May, and someone tried to misuse an exposed AWS SNS credential on 17 August. On 16 September an archive appeared on an online forum containing more than 130 repositories, including console and SaaS code, data-science models and deployment scripts. It also held 83 user email addresses and the names and emails of 51 potential investors from 2020. CrowdSec says no client data was exposed, no infrastructure or databases were compromised and no production code was altered. It rotated credentials on 16–17 September with GitHub’s help. The timeline is the lesson. A developer-tool supply-chain infection in May became a public leak four months later, through a token that was still valid after the developer had left. Update, 21 September: CrowdSec has publicly confirmed the scope. About 300 repositories were copied, roughly 170 of them private, including SaaS console source, AWS routines, connectors and automations. It attributes the access to a credential exposed by the TanStack infection, says no customer credentials or data were affected, that every potentially affected token has been rotated, and that no lateral movement was found.

_threatfeed.source_name: CrowdSec; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Leak 16 Sep 2026; reported 19 Sep 2026; scope confirmed 21 Sep 2026

items.title: BigCommerce merchants had shopper data pulled from their storefronts through a marketplace app’s stolen credentials — Master of Malt is the named victim, and BigCommerce says its own platform was not breached
items.content_text: BigCommerce has told merchants that credentials belonging to the third-party Ribon and Ribon 1.5 shopping-experience apps, operated by Be A Part Of, a brand of Fastr, were used between 13 and 17 September to inject malicious scripts into “a small number” of merchant storefronts. Rather than skimming cards at checkout, the scripts read existing customer records: names, email addresses, phone numbers and shipping addresses. BigCommerce says passwords and payment-card data are stored separately and were not affected, that its own systems were not compromised, and that it uninstalled the app from affected stores to cut off the attacker’s access, notified those merchants directly and is supplying log data to the developer. UK spirits retailer Master of Malt has confirmed it was affected and has written to customers; BleepingComputer reports the impact may extend to hundreds of other stores, and the merchant count has not been disclosed. No statement from the app developer had been located at the time of writing. This is the hosted-commerce version of the pattern the Brevo card describes: the platform was fine, the merchant’s own code was fine, and a third party’s credential did the damage. An app installed from a marketplace runs with whatever scope it was granted on the day, and a credential the app vendor loses is a credential you lost. Update, 22 September: SecurityWeek gives the timeline. The credentials were misused from 13 to 17 September, the key was revoked on 17 September and merchants were notified on the 18th. Master of Malt’s own investigation says the attackers pulled customer data “page by page” until the key was revoked, and it makes no mention of card data. Neither the app developer nor its parent had commented.

_threatfeed.source_name: BigCommerce statement via BleepingComputer; Master of Malt customer notice; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Incident 13–17 Sep 2026; confirmed 17 Sep 2026; reported 21 Sep 2026; timeline update 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Have I Been Pwned has independently verified 6.4 million people in the McKesson data — the 284 million the extortion group claims remains a claim
items.content_text: McKesson, one of the largest pharmaceutical and medical-supply distributors in the United States, confirmed at the end of August that an attacker had gained unauthorised access to third-party applications tied to its Oncology & Multispecialty and Medical-Surgical business units. The extortion group ShinyHunters demanded roughly $55 million by 1 September, McKesson did not pay, and the data was published. The number that matters arrived on 10 September and it came from neither side: Have I Been Pwned analysed the leaked dataset independently and verified approximately 6.4 million affected individuals, with names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, employer details and health information among the exposed fields. ShinyHunters claims 284 million records. HIBP could not substantiate that figure, and could not substantiate the Social Security numbers the group also claimed to hold. Both numbers belong on the page, because the distance between them is the lesson: an extortion group’s stated record count is a negotiating position, routinely inflated by counting rows, duplicates and unrelated files rather than people, and it is the number that reaches the headlines first. The verified 6.4 million is the figure to plan against, and it is serious enough without help. McKesson says core distribution services remain operational and is offering credit monitoring to those affected.

_threatfeed.source_name: McKesson; Have I Been Pwned; SecurityWeek; The Register; HIPAA Journal
_threatfeed.date_note: Breach disclosed 31 Aug 2026; scope independently verified 10 Sep 2026

items.title: Revolut was tricked into handing over identity documents and full transaction history by an attacker impersonating a government agency — no software flaw was involved
items.content_text: Revolut disclosed on 14 September that an unauthorised party impersonated a government agency and, using what the company describes as valid technical domain credentials, submitted fraudulent data requests that its process treated as legitimate. The exposed fields for the affected subset of customers are unusually complete: names, addresses, dates of birth, copies of driving licences and passports, identity-verification selfies, IBANs, account statements and full transaction history including cryptocurrency activity. Revolut says customer funds and core systems were not affected, has blocked the attacker’s email, and has notified law enforcement, data-protection authorities and financial regulators while contacting affected users directly. The number of people affected has not been disclosed. Update, 17–18 September: SecurityWeek and American Banker have reported the scale and the route in, drawing on Hudson Rock and other investigators rather than on Revolut. They put the affected group at about 680 high-value customers, none of them in the US. The forged requests ran for five to six months from an Italian Ministry of the Interior certified-email (PEC) account compromised by infostealer malware, and went to Revolut Bank UAB in Lithuania. An actor calling itself “IAmNotAVillain” has posted a US$3 million demand; reports date the post to 16 or 18 September. Revolut says it has received no direct contact or demand, and still describes the affected group only as “a limited number of customers”. Update, 20–21 September: American Banker reports that the PEC credentials are believed to have been bought from infostealer logs, and that Revolut has notified data-protection authorities and financial regulators. Malwarebytes, via Infosecurity Magazine, has observed a smishing wave against Revolut customers that began on 14 September, days after Revolut began telling affected users; the messages inject into the genuine Revolut SMS thread, request camera access and mimic the app’s video identity check before asking for the password. Malwarebytes links the wave to data from this breach, which is its assessment rather than Revolut’s. What makes this worth the space on an all-IT page is that there is nothing to patch. The compromised control was an authorisation decision inside a legal-request workflow — a queue where the operating assumption is that the requester is who the letterhead says, and where refusing or delaying feels like obstructing an investigation. Any organisation with a channel through which police, regulators or government agencies can lawfully demand customer data has the same queue, usually staffed by a small team under time pressure, and usually without the verification step that would have stopped this.

_threatfeed.source_name: Revolut; SecurityWeek; American Banker; Infosecurity Magazine; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Sep 2026; scale and vector reported 17–18 Sep 2026; smishing wave reported 21 Sep 2026

items.title: One of Germany’s largest universities says an attacker took the data students supplied at enrolment — bank details and health-insurance numbers included
items.content_text: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München said on 21 September that an unknown attacker gained access to a server holding the information students provide when they enrol: names, dates of birth, contact details and university email addresses, bank account details, health-insurance numbers, BAföG student-aid identifiers, educational history and, in some cases, the reasons given for a leave of absence. LMU says it “must currently assume that this data was in fact retrieved”. It has isolated the server, taken other systems offline as a precaution, engaged external forensic specialists, notified the Bavarian state criminal police and the supervisory authorities, and is monitoring criminal forums for the data. Examination records and course content were not affected. No number of affected students has been given, no actor has claimed the intrusion and no ransom demand has been reported; the university’s statement puts detection on 19 September. For enterprises the useful detail is the data class. Enrolment data is collected once, retained for years and rarely looked at, which is exactly the kind of store that ends up on a server nobody thought of as sensitive. Bank details plus a date of birth and an insurance identifier are enough for convincing invoice and benefits fraud against the individuals concerned, so LMU’s forum monitoring is the right instinct, and an organisation holding similar data for its own staff should know which server it is on today.

_threatfeed.source_name: LMU newsroom statement; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Detected 19 Sep 2026; announced 21 Sep 2026

items.title: A Wyoming bank has restored online and mobile banking two weeks after a cyber incident it still has not explained — and a data-centre cooling failure took 23 credit unions down the same month with no attacker at all
items.content_text: Hilltop National Bank, a US$1.14 billion community bank in Casper, Wyoming, saw systems degrade on 8 September, confirmed an incident and took all systems offline on 9 September, and was still without online and mobile banking and its website a week later, according to American Banker. Scheduled bill payments were suspended, debit-card withdrawals were capped at US$1,000 a day and seven of eight branches were on limited transactions, with local coverage later reporting most branches reopened. The bank notified the OCC and the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City under the 36-hour computer-security incident rule. It has not called the event ransomware, no leak-site claim has been seen, and it has made no statement about customer data; chief executive Darren Cantlay acknowledged the incident in a video message. Separately, on 15 September a cooling failure at Ark Data Centers in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, which hosts the Sharetec core-processing platform, knocked 23 credit unions in 14 states offline; Sharetec’s notices to members said backup systems “did not have time to take over”. The affected institutions hold about US$2.56 billion in assets and serve roughly 200,000 members, and at least one closed for the duration. That one is not an attack, but from a member’s chair it looks identical, and the NCUA has noted that it lacks authority to examine third-party processors. The common lesson is about the recovery plan rather than the cause: a small institution that runs on a hosted core has no independent way to serve customers when that core stops, whoever stopped it. Update, 21–22 September: Hilltop’s own update site says personal online and mobile banking returned on 21 September, and business online banking, with ACH and transfer templates, and the business mobile app on 22 September. In-branch debit-card replacement is available. Business positive pay is still offline. Transactions from the outage were processed manually and a backlog is still being worked through. The bank has still disclosed neither a cause nor any data exposure.

_threatfeed.source_name: American Banker; K2 Radio; Hilltop Bank update site; Oil City News; Sharetec member notices via American Banker
_threatfeed.date_note: Hilltop incident 8–9 Sep 2026, reported 15 Sep 2026, services restored 21–22 Sep 2026; Sharetec outage 15 Sep 2026, reported 21 Sep 2026

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms customer data was taken through an external-facing system — the 7.49 million record count is the attacker’s claim, and electric and gas delivery were not affected
items.content_text: Houston-based CenterPoint Energy, which serves about 7 million customers across Texas, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio, said in an SEC 8-K filed on 14 September under Item 8.01 (other events), not Item 1.05, the item for material cybersecurity incidents, that an unauthorised third party obtained customer personal information through one of its external-facing systems. The company learned of it after someone posted online claiming to hold the data. It confirms that names, account information, billing information and the last four digits of Social Security numbers were taken for a portion of customers, says electric and gas delivery has not been impacted, and does not expect a material financial impact; outside experts are engaged and law enforcement and regulators have been notified. An actor claims to have pulled about 7.49 million records by abusing a public API with no rate limiting and has leaked a 2.5 GB archive. Neither CenterPoint nor the outlets reporting it have verified that count, and BleepingComputer puts the intrusion window at roughly 17 August to 1 September. The actor also threatened to go after the company’s “main infrastructure” next time; that is an unverified threat, and nothing reported so far indicates any operational impact. Help Net Security reported on 16 September that multiple class actions have been filed; CenterPoint has still not given a confirmed victim count. The lesson for enterprise IT is the entry point: a customer-facing interface that answered too many questions, too quickly, for too long without anyone noticing.

_threatfeed.source_name: CenterPoint Energy SEC 8-K; BleepingComputer; The Record; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed via 8-K; reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: A trusted plugin update was the attack: Admin Menu Editor Pro’s own update server shipped a backdoor — the vendor counts about 230 customers and at least 1,500 sites affected, and a clean 2.37 is out
items.content_text: An attacker gained access to the server hosting adminmenueditor.com and used the premium WordPress plugin’s normal update mechanism to push a malicious version 2.35 of Admin Menu Editor Pro between roughly 06:00 and 13:00 UTC on 14 September. The replacement, version 2.36, was also compromised later the same day. The developer confirmed the incident in a notice on the vendor site. It counts about 230 customers affected in the initial compromise, with several hundred more possibly affected depending on when they downloaded. Correction: the previous edition said the “1,500 sites” figure was BleepingComputer’s rather than the vendor’s. BleepingComputer’s report of at least 1,500 compromised sites is in fact sourced to developer Janis Elsts’ analysis of his own update-server logs, so both numbers are vendor-sourced: customers hold licences that cover several sites each. The vendor site itself was still “temporarily offline” on 22 September. The vendor says the attacker may have obtained root-level access to the distribution server, and on 19 September it released a clean version 2.37, built from 2.34. The backdoor drops a web shell at includes/wp-user-consent.php, creates a /wp-content/object-cache/ directory and wp_ocache* database options, and adds a hidden administrator account whose name begins with wp_. The vendor’s fuller list adds a cron hook _wp_cconsent_tick, a plugin named wordpress-cache-optimizer and a user wpsecuresuppbot. Version 2.34 is confirmed clean. There is no CVE, because nothing in the plugin’s code was vulnerable: the distribution channel was the flaw, and every site that did the responsible thing and auto-updated received the payload first.

_threatfeed.source_name: Admin Menu Editor developer notice (vendor site offline as of 22 Sep 2026); BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Compromise 14 Sep 2026; site count reported 15 Sep 2026; clean 2.37 on 19 Sep 2026

items.title: IDScan.net has confirmed the breach it was being sued over — 153 million driving-licence scans plus ID cards, travel documents and medical cards, with the FBI investigating
items.content_text: This item has changed state. IDScan.net, the identity-verification vendor used by banks, car rental firms, retailers, cannabis dispensaries, gun shops and hospitality businesses to check government-issued ID, has confirmed unauthorised access to its cloud platform. The intrusion was discovered around 1 September and disclosed on 4 September; the exposure is put at more than 153 million driving-licence scans, along with roughly 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents and 579,000 medical cards. It was first surfaced by Brian Krebs after the data was advertised on a dark-web marketplace called “Nexus”, and the FBI is investigating. That moves it from the litigation reporting this page carried last week to a confirmed vendor breach at very large scale. The reason it belongs on an all-IT page rather than in a sector column is that almost nobody chose to hold this data themselves. Age and identity verification is being pushed into more consumer and workplace flows by regulation and by platform policy, and each requirement creates another vendor holding scanned government identity documents on behalf of businesses that never wanted a repository. That data is the most durable a person has — a licence number and a scanned document cannot be rotated the way a password can — and the notification obligation tends to follow the business that chose the vendor, not only the vendor. Update, 22 September: the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Philippe Dufresne, has opened an investigation into IDScan.net’s security practices and whether its breach notifications were adequate under federal private-sector privacy law. The number of Canadians affected has not been disclosed, and IDScan did not respond to The Record. It is the first regulator action reported on this breach.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; Krebs on Security; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Breach confirmed 10 Sep 2026; first reported ~1–4 Sep 2026; Canadian OPC investigation 22 Sep 2026

items.title: MikroTik routers are being taken over through exposed SSH — CERT Polska names the chain MikroTrick and gives you a one-line indicator to check for
items.content_text: CERT Polska warned that MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities are being actively exploited against devices with SSH reachable from the internet, with attacks occurring since at least 2 September 2026. Six issues were disclosed; the chain being used, which the CERT calls MikroTrick, combines CVE-2026-67276, an SSH authentication bypass rated CVSS 9.2, with CVE-2026-86060, an SSH privilege escalation through a crafted username also rated 9.2, to give an unauthenticated attacker full control of the device. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277, is a memory disclosure issue in the bandwidth-test service rated 8.8. Fixes are in RouterOS 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. The useful part of the advisory is the detection guidance: log entries showing a login failure for user “-2”, or an account added by ssh:-2@<ip>, indicate exploitation attempts, and the presence of a privileged account named “ops” indicates the device is already compromised. CERT Polska named 82.192.72.4 and 103.102.31.18 among the attacking sources. Cybernews reported roughly 122,500 exposed routers; patching alone does not evict an attacker who already has an account. KEV status, corrected: CISA added CVE-2026-86060, the privilege-escalation half of the chain, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 September with a 13 September deadline, now passed. CVE-2026-67276, the authentication bypass, was not in the catalog as of the 21 September catalog version.

_threatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska advisory; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Cybernews
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation since at least 2 Sep 2026; reported 6–7 Sep 2026; CVE-2026-86060 KEV-listed 10 Sep 2026

items.title: Telus has told customers that attackers were logging into their accounts with valid credentials from February 2025 to June 2026 — sixteen months before disclosure
items.content_text: The Canadian telecommunications operator notified customers on 14 September of a campaign in which attackers used compromised credentials to sign into subscriber accounts and view or modify billing, subscription and contact details. In some cases they attempted to port service to a competing provider or altered subscriptions outright. Exposed data reported includes names, account numbers, phone numbers, billing addresses, partial card numbers and payment history. Telus has not disclosed how many accounts were affected, and has not said whether the credentials came from an internal compromise or from credential stuffing against reused passwords — a distinction that matters, because one is a breach of Telus and the other is a breach of its customers that Telus failed to absorb. The company has reset affected credentials, notified Vancouver Police and is offering identity-theft protection. The duration is the part worth studying: sixteen months of successful logins with valid credentials produced no detection, which is what account takeover looks like when monitoring is built around failed authentication rather than around the behaviour that follows a successful one. For enterprises the parallel is the customer or partner portal, which is usually the least-instrumented authentication surface in the estate.

_threatfeed.source_name: Telus; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Sep 2026; campaign ran Feb 2025 – Jun 2026

items.title: Florida’s driver database was accessed with credentials stolen from a law-enforcement officer’s personal device — no vulnerability was involved at any stage
items.content_text: Florida officials confirmed on 11 September that the state’s DAVID driver-record system was accessed using credentials taken from a law-enforcement officer’s personal device. There was no exploit, no unpatched server and no zero-day: the attacker logged in. Update, 16 September: ShinyHunters has published hundreds of thousands of the stolen files on its leak site, saying the state did not pay. TechCrunch reviewed a copy and describes vehicle ownership certificates carrying names, addresses and VINs, with Social Security numbers and non-US passports and immigration papers in a subset, and no driving-licence images or photos. The Record had already linked the intrusion to ShinyHunters, the same extortion group behind the McKesson breach above, which makes the week’s two largest identity-data incidents a matched pair driven by credentials rather than code. The state has not published a final affected-record count; credential revocation, a review of multi-factor authentication on law-enforcement data access and notification processes are under way. The uncomfortable structure here is one most enterprises share. A high-value data system is reachable by a population of privileged users who sit outside the organisation that owns the data, on devices that organisation does not manage, with an authentication decision it does not control. That describes a police officer and a state driver database; it equally describes a contractor, a franchisee, a distributor or a clinical partner reaching your customer or patient records from a laptop you have never inspected.

_threatfeed.source_name: Florida officials; TechCrunch; BleepingComputer; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Confirmed 11 Sep 2026; data published 16 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers turned MemTensor’s own GitHub Actions release workflows against it, took its npm and PyPI publish tokens, and shipped a self-spreading credential stealer
items.content_text: Aikido, SafeDep, Socket and StepSecurity reported on 23 September that attackers pushed commits that made MemTensor’s release workflows hand over its npm and PyPI publishing tokens. They then published malicious versions of @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin (0.1.21, 0.1.23 and 0.1.25) on npm and MemoryOS 2.0.34 on PyPI, which has since been quarantined. The payload, sckit, is a Go credential stealer for Windows, Linux and macOS. It takes .npmrc files, Vault tokens, SSH keys and AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Hugging Face, Slack, Stripe and SendGrid secrets, and uses any publishing rights it finds to push itself into more packages. The command-and-control domain is skyleen[.]fr. Download counts were not given, and the packages are niche tooling for AI-agent memory. The technique is what matters. The packages were published by the project’s own pipeline, so provenance checks would pass, the same weakness as the GHAPPIER case on this page. No attribution has been made.

_threatfeed.source_name: Aikido; SafeDep; Socket; StepSecurity; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Malicious releases and reports 23 Sep 2026

items.title: The first known malicious Terraform providers on the HashiCorp Registry deliver Go malware with blockchain and Slack command-and-control — researchers link them to North Korea’s fake-interview campaign
items.content_text: Aikido reported on 23 September two malicious Terraform providers on the HashiCorp Registry: kreuzwenker/docker, a typosquat of the widely used kreuzwerker/docker provider with 1,449 downloads, and gocommunity-io/dockerd with 222. It also found two Go modules, gocommunity.io/orderedbtree and gogets.dev/btreex. They deliver Go malware that uses the Ethereum Sepolia test network and Slack for command-and-control. The Hacker News describes this as the first known malicious payload delivery through the Terraform registry. The researchers link it to Graphalgo, a fake-recruiter campaign that ReversingLabs tied to North Korea in February. That link is researcher-assessed overlap, not an official attribution. HashiCorp had not commented in the reporting, and removal status was not stated. It is a different cluster from the TraderTraitor lock-file case on this page, but the target is the same: infrastructure engineers, whose laptops hold cloud credentials with production reach. A misspelt provider source in a .tf file is enough.

_threatfeed.source_name: Aikido; The Hacker News; ReversingLabs (Graphalgo background)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Talos reports CLOSEDQUORUM, a Windows implant that asks up to four AI models what to do next and acts on their consensus — research, not a mass campaign
items.content_text: Cisco Talos published on 22 September what it calls “the first reported autonomous AI C2 implant”. CLOSEDQUORUM is Windows malware that sends its situation to up to four large language models, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen and Mistral, and acts on the action they agree on, instead of waiting for an operator’s command. Talos also released CAIRN, a toolkit for tracking this kind of malware. It is a different thing from the attack framework named “Cairn” in the skimming report on this page. No victim count or campaign scale is given. This is on the page as an early signal. Malware that decides its own next step makes less of the usual operator traffic, and it needs an outbound path to public AI APIs. Most enterprises do not yet watch that path.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco Talos; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Seven agencies in four countries say North Korea’s WaterPlum infected more than 30,000 devices with fake job interviews — developers and IT staff are the target
items.content_text: Seven agencies in four countries issued a joint alert on 18 September about the North Korean group WaterPlum, also known as Contagious Interview: Japan’s National Police Agency and National Cybersecurity Office, the FBI, the US Defense Department’s Cyber Crime Center, Australia’s ACSC, and Germany’s BND and BfV. Between December 2025 and July 2026 the group infected at least 30,000 devices in more than 100 countries. It drained more than 7,000 cryptocurrency wallets of about ¥1.7 billion, roughly US$10.71 million. The method is the fake job interview. Operators pose as AI, cryptocurrency and NFT companies, or approach candidates through recruiting and freelance platforms, then ask applicants to download and run a project as a technical test. The projects deliver BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret, OtterCookie, OtterCandy and StoatWaffle; StoatWaffle runs through VS Code tasks. Japanese police and the FBI attribute WaterPlum, and some North Korean IT workers, to the 313 General Bureau of the Munitions Industry Department. The alert also covers the IT-worker scheme, which uses AI face-swapping and text-to-speech in video interviews and stolen identity documents to get real jobs. BleepingComputer adds that Japanese authorities have, for the first time, dismantled a North Korean IT-worker operation inside Japan, with evidence of “several hundred million yen” sent abroad. The targets are developers, engineers and IT staff, so the infected device can be a work machine, or a personal one that holds work credentials. Update, 21 September: the Rust project’s security team has warned crates.io maintainers and owners of popular crates that they are being approached by fake recruiters who move to a video call and then ask the target to install a “missing audio codec”; it links the approach to the August hijack of the arrayref crate and attributes the style to North Korea without naming a unit. SentinelLabs’ report on a different North Korean unit, TraderTraitor, using the same lure has its own card below.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI/IC3 joint alert; The Record; BleepingComputer; Rust security team via SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Joint alert 18 Sep 2026; Rust security warning 21 Sep 2026

items.title: North Korea’s TraderTraitor put its LayerZero-era macOS backdoors on a DevOps engineer at an Indian IT services firm — the lure was a Terraform lock file in a fake interview project
items.content_text: SentinelLabs reported on 18 September that FLATROOF and ROOFDECK, the Rust macOS backdoors first seen in the LayerZero bridge intrusion, were found on the Mac of a DevOps engineer at a small India-based IT services provider with no cryptocurrency business. The engineer had taken a fake job interview whose take-home project contained a weaponised .terraform.lock.hcl; running terraform init pulled a malicious custom provider. The backdoors, deployed as “SystemUpdate” and “iSync”, run shell commands, harvest AWS and Google Cloud credentials and exfiltrate over Telegram and Nostr relays; ROOFDECK persists through a LaunchAgent masquerading as a Chrome renderer process. Beaconing began on 29 March, with an updated variant on 20 April. SentinelLabs attributes the activity to TraderTraitor, also tracked as UNC4899 and Jade Sleet, a different North Korean unit from the WaterPlum group in the joint advisory above, using the same fake-interview playbook. The victim is not named and downstream customer impact is not discussed. The choice of target is the point: an IT services provider’s DevOps engineer holds cloud credentials for many clients, so one personal decision to run an interview task on a work laptop becomes a supply-chain position.

_threatfeed.source_name: SentinelLabs; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Report 18 Sep 2026; reported 21 Sep 2026

items.title: Fake “LastPass Authenticator” GitHub pages deliver a Microsoft-signed kernel driver that kills 145 security products, then the Rapuncel infostealer
items.content_text: LastPass’s threat-intelligence team and Delphos Labs reported on 17 September a campaign in which search-ranked fraudulent GitHub organisations and GitHub Pages sites, such as one named LastPass-Authenticator, impersonate at least 40 software brands and redirect visitors to attacker servers serving ZIP installers padded to 127–148 MB to get past size-limited scanners. The installer loads a kernel driver, Alinubx.sys, a renamed copy of a driver from a Chinese disk-encryption product that was signed through the Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher chain in March 2023 and is installed as an “NVIDIA File System Filter Driver”. From kernel mode it terminates processes from a list of 145 antivirus and EDR products. The Rapuncel stealer then harvests passwords and cookies from more than 20 browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord, Steam and Telegram sessions, Windows Credential Manager and any file whose name suggests a password, seed phrase or recovery code. LastPass says the signature had not been revoked and the driver was not on Microsoft’s vulnerable-driver blocklist at the time of writing; the lure was first seen in August and was still live in September, and no victim count is known. It is on this page because the driver defeats the one control most enterprises rely on to notice an infostealer, and because the lure is exactly what a well-meaning employee types into a search engine when nobody has told them where the authenticator app comes from.

_threatfeed.source_name: LastPass and Delphos Labs report; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Report 17 Sep 2026; reported 18–21 Sep 2026

items.title: Ten npm packages hid their payload in library code that runs only when the package is used — built to get past the install-script blocking GitHub introduced in June
items.content_text: Checkmarx has reported indexed-btree, an npm package impersonating the legitimate sorted-btree library, and nine related packages: ordered-kv-index, btree-leaderboard, priority-slot-queue, btree-range-store, btree-core, btree-time-index, btree-lru-cache, neighbor-key-map and sliding-score-window. All ten have been removed from npm. The malicious code does not use preinstall, install or postinstall scripts. It sits inside BTree.prototype.set() and runs when an application actually calls the library, so it slips past the install-script blocking GitHub announced in June 2026. Once running, it collects host details such as hostname, architecture, CPU, memory and uptime and sends them to Slack and Telegram. It fetches commands from a smart contract on the Ethereum Sepolia test network, decrypts a second stage using X25519 key exchange and AES, and can delete files and remove its own triggers. The download figures reported for these packages are likely inflated and have not been independently verified, so they are not repeated here. Checkmarx has not disclosed how many systems ran the code or what the second stage does; its write-up, dated 17 September, does give the Sepolia contract address, 0xE390863Dac96a7118C71227C2b099B50cF602D31, and notes that the source repository was still online after the packages were removed. The lesson is the evasion. Blocking install scripts closes one door, and this campaign used the next one: code that runs inside your application, your tests or your build.

_threatfeed.source_name: Checkmarx; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Checkmarx research 17 Sep 2026; reported 20 Sep 2026

items.title: An npm package published with valid GitHub Actions provenance carried a loader that runs only when the MCP server starts — Trusted Publishing was abused, not bypassed
items.content_text: CloudSEK reported on 20 September that an attacker with stolen maintainer credentials for the @dforge-core/dforge-mcp npm package changed its CI workflow to publish automatically on push, then shipped malicious versions 0.2.20 and 0.2.21 on 9 September. Because the publish went through the normal GitHub Actions pipeline, the packages carried a valid OIDC provenance attestation; version 0.2.21 was live for about 35 minutes. The payload, which CloudSEK names GHAPPIER, does not run at install time. It executes when the Model Context Protocol server launches, which sidesteps install-script scanning and quarantine in the same way as the runtime-only btree packages on the card above. The loader has been found in 65 public repositories, 73 files and 22 accounts, and its second stage overlaps with the PolinRider campaign that other researchers attribute to North Korea. The scale of downstream victims is unknown. In a related case, Socket reported on 17 September that PolinRider had compromised the GitHub organisation behind the Packagist package visanduma/nova-two-factor and force-pushed malicious code into its development branches, with no tagged stable release found affected. Provenance attestations prove that a package was built by a given workflow from a given commit. They do not prove the workflow was still under the maintainer’s control, and a workflow is one of the things a stolen credential can change.

_threatfeed.source_name: CloudSEK via Infosecurity Magazine; Socket
_threatfeed.date_note: CloudSEK report 20 Sep 2026; Socket report 17 Sep 2026

items.title: “Plugin4Shell”: the major AI coding agents pinned plugins to a commit SHA but never checked they got it — a branch named after the SHA wins, and auto-update makes it zero-click
items.content_text: Researchers at AIR Security published on 17 September a flaw pattern they call Plugin4Shell affecting Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot and Gemini CLI. Each tool installs plugins from a Git repository pinned to a commit hash, and each checked out the pin without confirming the resulting tree was that commit. An attacker who controls the plugin repository creates a branch named identically to the pinned SHA and makes it the default; git checkout resolves the name to the branch, and the tool installs the attacker’s code while the pin appears to be honoured. Because the tools auto-update plugins in the background, no user action is needed. Patch status differs by vendor, so read it plainly: Anthropic fixed Claude Code in version 2.1.179 and Codex was fixed in 0.146.0; the researchers say GitHub Copilot has no fix and that Google has described Gemini CLI as deprecated and will not fix it. A working proof of concept exists; no in-the-wild exploitation is claimed and no CVE is cited. This dashboard is itself compiled with Claude, which is a reason to state the patch status plainly rather than softly. The general lesson holds for any system that pins dependencies by hash: a pin is only a control if something verifies the hash after the fetch.

_threatfeed.source_name: AIR Security; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 17 Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026

items.title: Spain’s data protection authority has received its first breach notification in which the attack was carried out by an AI agent — and the chain was ordinary
items.content_text: Spain’s data protection authority, the AEPD, says it has received its first personal-data breach notification involving an attack carried out with an autonomous AI agent. In the AEPD’s account, a third party used the agent “as an instrument”. The agent searched generic files for vulnerabilities, logged in with credentials it found there, located a flaw in an application, modified personal-data records and accessed invoices. The attacker used a well-known language model that the AEPD does not name, and the authority says this does not mean the model or its provider was compromised. The victim and its sector are not disclosed. Reports differ on how much a human directed each step, so the AEPD’s own wording is the safest guide. Deputy director Francisco Pérez Bes says one notification is not a trend, but it is a sign that AI-supported attacks “have ceased to be a theoretical risk”. Spain’s CCN has published guidance on offensive AI that covers faster patching, identity protection, supplier oversight and agent governance. The point to take away is how ordinary the chain is: found credentials, an application flaw and altered records. An agent simply does each step faster, and each step is covered by a control most organisations already have.

_threatfeed.source_name: AEPD; Help Net Security; Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: AEPD blog 14 Sep 2026; reported 17–18 Sep 2026

items.title: The GRIMWEDGE campaign chained two Chrome zero-days and a Windows ALPC bug through a compromised university website — the target was NGOs, the exposure is anyone running unpatched Chrome
items.content_text: Researchers disclosed on 15 September a campaign running since 1 September in which spear-phishing emails sent to non-governmental organisations linked to a compromised US university website, where a reflected cross-site-scripting flaw redirected visitors into a three-zero-day exploit chain. Two of the flaws are in Chrome — CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491, the V8 and sandbox-escape bugs Google patched as its seventh in-the-wild zero-day of the year — and the third is CVE-2026-85880, the Windows ALPC elevation-of-privilege flaw that appeared in this month’s Patch Tuesday as an already-exploited zero-day. The chain delivers GRIMWEDGE, a multi-stage JavaScript backdoor capable of reconnaissance, file and process management and command execution, alongside a credential stealer tracked as LONGTALE. Attribution to the China-linked cluster UTA0560, overlapping with JungleBamboo and APT31, is researcher-assessed rather than official. The detail that generalises beyond the victims is the patch gap: fixes existed in the open-source Chromium code before they reached stable Chrome, and the attackers worked inside that interval. A browser is not patched because a fix has been committed, only because the build has shipped and the browser has been restarted. Update, 21 September: Volexity reports that a second China-linked cluster, UTA0565, used the same three-CVE chain through the BlueMoon kit on 3–4 September, while the flaws were still zero-days. It sent Chinese- and English-language phishing to Asian government entities, using lookalike sites impersonating the Center for American Progress (americanprgoress[.]top) and China Digital Times (chinadigitaltimes[.]top). The payload is a new backdoor, CLEANGULP, with shell, file-transfer and BOF-execution features and command-and-control at thecovnresation[.]com. The NGO and media brands were impersonated, not breached. A second group running the same chain fits the shared-kit picture on the Chrome card.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; Volexity; Google Chrome release notes; Microsoft security bulletins
_threatfeed.date_note: Campaign from 1 Sep 2026; disclosed 15 Sep 2026; Volexity UTA0565 report 21 Sep 2026

items.title: Red Heron automated a two-month-old Gitea exploit, scanned 1,386 instances and compromised 11 organisations — every victim was running a version patched in July
items.content_text: Researchers disclosed on 14 September that a group tracked as Red Heron built a public proof-of-concept for CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote code execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, into a Python framework that registers its own accounts, exploits unpatched servers, steals repositories and cleans up behind itself. It scanned 1,386 Gitea instances across seven countries and Acronis, whose research team published the findings, confirmed compromises at 11 organisations in five countries — the United States, Taiwan, Canada, Argentina and Sri Lanka (some coverage gives 13 across six), spanning defence, elections, energy, aerospace, telecommunications and government. At one Taiwanese victim the group reached root on a three-node Proxmox cluster and deployed a custom Linux rootkit, SIXZUT, that patches fifteen kernel functions to hide its activity. Attribution to China is assessed at moderate confidence. The flaw was disclosed and fixed in July, which is the point worth carrying: this is not a zero-day campaign but an industrialised sweep of everyone who did not patch, and self-hosted developer tooling — stood up by a team, owned by nobody, absent from the asset register — is where that population concentrates. Update, 21 September: GreyNoise’s report on the “Kapibala” actor, covered on the Zyxel card under Critical Advisories, lists the same Gitea flaw among that actor’s targets and infers an overlap with Red Heron through shared command-and-control and malware. GreyNoise presents that as an inference, and this card does not merge the two.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; researcher reporting
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploitation from 29 Jul 2026; disclosed 14 Sep 2026

items.title: ShinyHunters hijacked Clop’s leak site and is escalating its demands — the takeover is confirmed, the defacement has since come down, and the claimed theft of Clop’s data and keys is still unverified
items.content_text: The extortion group ShinyHunters, behind the McKesson and Florida DAVID incidents on this page, has defaced the Tor data-leak site of the Clop ransomware operation. BleepingComputer confirmed the defacement and an uploaded file reading “THIS SITE HAS BEEN PWN3D BY SHINYHUNTERES”. Everything else is ShinyHunters’ own claim, which BleepingComputer has not verified. The group says it got in through an unauthenticated file-upload flaw in the Grav CMS running the site. It also says it stole source code, plugins, system logs and the site’s onion-service private keys. ShinyHunters has given Clop 72 hours to make contact, and ties the feud to its allegation that Clop stole its Oracle E-Business Suite exploit in 2025. Clop has not responded. There is nothing for most defenders to do here, and the claims should be treated as claims. The story is carried as a signal about the ecosystem. The logs on a leak-site server can hold operator addresses and victim-negotiation traffic. If the key theft is real, Clop has lost control of its own identity on Tor. And one extortion crew publicly attacking another makes any data either group publishes less predictable. Update, 20–21 September: ShinyHunters has escalated, demanding everything Clop earned from its 2025 Oracle E-Business Suite campaign “with interest” plus a public apology, with the demand rising every 24 hours, and threatening to publish which companies paid Clop, how much, and to which Bitcoin addresses. Dark Reading reported on 21 September that the defacement had been removed and replaced by a plain-text note, possibly from Clop, saying ShinyHunters’ contact address does not work. Two researchers told Reuters the dispute appears genuine. There is still no independent verification that any victim or payment data was taken, so the threat to expose past payers remains a threat. On 21–22 September the same group defaced the FBI’s jobs portal (see that card).

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; DataBreaches.net; Dark Reading; The Register; The Record
_threatfeed.date_note: Defacement 19 Sep 2026; demands escalated 20–21 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers are phishing people into registering the attacker’s passkey on their Microsoft account — the mechanism sold as phishing-resistant, defeated by consent rather than by cryptography
items.content_text: Researchers described on 13 September two related campaigns against Microsoft 365 and cloud accounts. One is volume fraud: more than a million scam emails aimed at ACH and wire payment redirection. The second is the interesting one. Rather than trying to capture a credential or relay a token, the attacker walks the victim through registering an attacker-controlled passkey on the victim’s own account, using passkey-themed social engineering that borrows the language of a legitimate security upgrade. Nothing about the cryptography fails; the victim authorises the enrolment. The result is durable account access that survives a password reset and does not look like a compromise in the sign-in logs, because from the platform’s perspective the account simply has an additional valid authenticator. This does not make passkeys a bad control — they remain the strongest widely-available answer to credential phishing — but it moves the attack from the authentication event to the enrolment event, which is where most organisations have thought least.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News; researcher reporting
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 13 Sep 2026

items.title: The Check Point VPN flaw the Dutch NCSC warned about is now exploited — Check Point has seen attacks on Spark firewalls since 12 September, and CISA gave federal agencies until 25 September
items.content_text: This card has changed state. CVE-2026-85102, rated CVSS 9.8, is improper validation of certificate data during VPN negotiation on Check Point Security Gateways and Spark firewalls. It gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution. Check Point released fixes on 9 September (sk1000117). In an advisory on 22 September it said: “Starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers.” Spark is the SMB line, locally or centrally managed, and Help Net Security reports the attempts came from anonymisation infrastructure and were aimed at small businesses and managed service providers. CISA added the flaw to the KEV catalog on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September. Check Point gives no customer count and no attribution. It has published usable indicators: exploit certificates with subjects CN=vpn, CN=vpn-user or CN=vpnuser, with OU=users and O=global. The companion flaw from the same NCSC warning, CVE-2026-85103, a heap overflow in the VPN certificate decoder, was not part of the 22 September KEV additions. The previous edition said there was still a window before exploitation. That window closed on 12 September, ten days before the confirmation. The same Check Point advisory disclosed a second, separate exploited flaw in management servers, CVE-2026-93616.

_threatfeed.source_name: Check Point advisory; CISA KEV catalog; BleepingComputer; Help Net Security; Dutch NCSC
_threatfeed.date_note: Fixes 9 Sep 2026; exploitation from 12 Sep 2026; advisory and KEV listing 22 Sep 2026

items.title: A second Check Point management-server flaw, CVE-2026-93616, was exploited as a zero-day in July — it is not the over-long-username bug, it was fixed on 22 September, and you need to hunt back two months
items.content_text: Check Point’s 22 September advisory disclosed CVE-2026-93616, rated CVSS 9.8. It is a pre-authentication path traversal in the Security Management web service that lets an attacker execute scripts and load Java classes. Check Point says it saw a “handful of pinpointed attacks on July 23, 2026”, two months before the fix (sk1000171) became available on 22 September. Help Net Security lists the affected products as Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 22 September with a federal deadline of 25 September. Neither the targets nor the actor have been named. This is a different flaw from CVE-2026-91843, the over-long-username stack overflow on the card below, which is still not reported as exploited. Both are on the same servers, so one change window should close both. A management server pushes policy to every gateway beneath it, and this one was exploited for two months before anyone could patch.

_threatfeed.source_name: Check Point advisory; CISA KEV catalog; Help Net Security; The Hacker News; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Exploited 23 Jul 2026; fixed, disclosed and KEV-listed 22 Sep 2026

items.title: F5 BIG-IP APM has an exploited unauthenticated RCE, CVE-2026-94127 — only systems where APM acts as an OAuth authorization server are exposed, and the fixes are engineering hotfixes
items.content_text: F5 disclosed CVE-2026-94127 on 22 September (K000162605). It is a heap-based buffer overflow in BIG-IP Access Policy Manager, rated CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) and 9.3 (v4.0), which lets an unauthenticated attacker run code by sending crafted traffic to a virtual server. The condition is narrow. A system is exposed only when an access policy and an OAuth authorization server profile sit on the same virtual server, meaning APM is issuing OAuth tokens. Restricting the management interface does not help, because the attack arrives on the data plane, and Appliance mode systems are equally affected. F5 confirms exploitation but has not described the attacker, the victims or when it started. Rapid7 reported no confirmed public proof-of-concept as of 22 September. CISA added it to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. The fixes are engineering hotfixes for 21.1.0, 17.5.0–17.5.1 and 17.1.0–17.1.3, and F5 support can provide a temporary iRule mitigation. The OAuth configuration limits the number of exposed systems. The organisations that run APM this way are usually banks, government bodies and telecoms, where BIG-IP is the front door to single sign-on.

_threatfeed.source_name: F5 advisory K000162605; CISA KEV catalog; Rapid7; The Hacker News; CERT-EU
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed and KEV-listed 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator has an exploited maximum-severity flaw, CVE-2026-93952 — the SD-WAN controller that pushes configuration to every branch edge
items.content_text: Arista has disclosed CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation flaw in the certificate-based authentication between VeloCloud Edges and the VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO). BleepingComputer calls it maximum severity, and Arista’s advisory 0183 rates it CVSS 10.0 (v3.1). It is low complexity and needs no privileges or user interaction. The attacker does need network access to the VCO web interface and “the public portion of the VeloCloud Edge authentication certificate”, and certificate-based Edge authentication must be enabled. Arista says the issue “was discovered externally and is known to be actively exploited”. Affected versions are VCO 6.1.3.7 and earlier and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. The fixed releases are 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8 or later. Arista says hosted VCO has been updated, so this is mainly an on-premises problem. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 22 September with a 25 September deadline. Published indicators include connections from 142.93.149.77 and 104.248.126.159, an x-vc-opt HTTP header, and encoded characters or unusual paths in access logs. An orchestrator compromise matters because the orchestrator configures every edge beneath it: branch offices, shops, clinics and the managed-service customers of carriers.

items.title: WordPress core CVE-2026-87902 drew exploit attempts within five hours of its fix, and Patchstack saw traffic rise tenfold the next day — update to 7.1.2 even if you installed 7.1.1 last week
items.content_text: WordPress 7.1.2, released on 22 September with backports down to the 4.7 branch, fixes CVE-2026-87902. It is an unauthenticated path traversal that allows local PHP file inclusion and remote code execution, rated CVSS 9.2, and was found by Robert Ressl. Code execution needs two conditions. The active parent or child theme must have a top-level directory whose name starts with page- (such as page-templates), and there must be a readable PHP file outside the theme directories that can be abused. The advisory notes that the official PHP Docker image and the default cPanel configuration with PHP before 8.5 meet the second condition. Patchstack recorded the first malicious requests at 17:44 UTC on 22 September, under five hours after the patch. By 23 September the traffic had increased tenfold and moved from probing with double-encoded traversal strings to writing files such as wp-pear-rce-flag.php, poc87902.php, luci_*.php and zeta_*.php into /tmp and /var/tmp. No confirmed site compromises have been counted, and the flaw is not reported as KEV-listed. This is a different bug from Click2Shell, which was fixed in 7.1.1 and covered below. Sites updated to 7.1.1 last week still need 7.1.2.

_threatfeed.source_name: WordPress release notes; Patchstack; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Fixed 22 Sep 2026; exploitation from 22 Sep 2026; escalation reported 23 Sep 2026

items.title: Cisco ISE has a CVSS 10.0 zero-day under active exploitation — unauthenticated root on the system that decides who gets onto your network, with no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine that it describes as insufficient authentication control on an API endpoint. An unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the web management interface and get root command execution. ISE and ISE-PIC 3.0 through 3.5 are affected. Fixes are in 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 P11, 3.3 P12, 3.4 P7 and 3.5 P4, and there is no workaround. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, now passed. The advisory was still at its original revision on 21 September, and Cisco has published no exposure count. No actor has been named, and Cisco warns that attackers may “remove or hide evidence of exploitation”. This is the third actively exploited ISE flaw since June 2025, after CVE-2025-20281 and CVE-2025-20337. It is also Cisco’s second exploited zero-day in a matter of days, after the Secure Email Gateway flaw below. The product’s role is why this ranks just behind the lead story. ISE is the policy engine that decides which users and devices get onto the wired, wireless and VPN network, and what they can reach once there. VulnCheck notes that root on ISE lets an attacker rewrite network access policy, pull stored credentials, delete logs and move laterally. The control meant to contain an intruder ends up working for the intruder.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT; CISA KEV catalog; CyberScoop; The Hacker News; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory and KEV listing 16 Sep 2026; reported 17 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA added a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw patched in June to KEV on 21 September — GreyNoise ties it to one actor who pulled configs and root hashes from 996 switches in 48 countries, and stole 18,566 government records through WordPress
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 21 September with a federal deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel’s GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN side execute operating-system commands with a crafted HTTP request; Zyxel published fixed firmware, 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and per-model equivalents, on 16 June, and its advisory gives no CVSS score. The KEV entry says “LAN-based”, so exposure runs through management-plane reachability rather than the open internet. GreyNoise’s report the same day documents what it calls the first in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, active since 7 May and assessed as a Chinese speaker, used a PyArmor-obfuscated Python tool to exploit 996 GS1900 switches in 48 countries, led by Italy (133), the United States (129) and Taiwan (123), pulling configurations and root-level hashed credentials over TFTP; 564 of the victims still used factory-default credentials. The same actor exploited two WordPress flaws, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, to steal at least 18,566 records, including accounts, plaintext passwords and personal data tied to law-enforcement and government agencies, from an unnamed western government organisation on 22 July, and also worked UniFi OS, FlowiseAI, Gitea (CVE-2026-60004, the Red Heron flaw on this page), Nuclio, SENAITE LIMS, Proxmox VE and PAN-OS GlobalProtect. GreyNoise infers an overlap with Red Heron through shared command-and-control and malware, and infers LLM-assisted tooling from how the tool iterated; both are inferences. The GS1900 is a small-office switch. It sits in branch offices, schools, shops and labs, is bought without a security review and is rarely on a patch schedule, which is why a June fix is being exploited in September. Update, 22–24 September: BleepingComputer’s coverage of the GreyNoise research adds no new victims. The federal deadline is today, 24 September, and four more edge and management flaws joined KEV on 22 September (see the Check Point, F5 and Arista cards).

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; GreyNoise; Zyxel security advisory
_threatfeed.date_note: Zyxel advisory 16 Jun 2026; KEV-listed and GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; BleepingComputer 22 Sep 2026

items.title: Cisco’s firewall-management console has three attack clusters on it — one Sandworm-linked by tooling, one that deployed Qilin — and the hardening advisory, revised on 18 September, is not about exploited flaws
items.content_text: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center remains the clearest example this month of attackers going after the system that manages the perimeter. CVE-2026-20079 (CVSS 10.0) is an unauthenticated authentication bypass that gives root command execution through crafted HTTP requests; CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3) is a hardcoded low-privilege credential. Cisco Talos separates the activity into three clusters. UAT-12197, unattributed, uses CVE-2026-20079 to plant JSP web shells and a cmd.jar credential extractor. UAT-11823, which Talos tracks as an APT, chains both flaws and deployed a 64-bit Linux variant of Cyclops Blink, malware previously attributed to Sandworm. Talos says the cluster’s tooling overlaps with Sandworm’s, which makes it Sandworm-linked, not a Sandworm attribution. UAT-11988, assessed with high confidence as a ransomware operator whose tradecraft matches Qilin affiliates, entered through CVE-2026-20316 alone and deployed Qilin on selected endpoints. CISA added CVE-2026-20079 to KEV on 9 September with a 12 September deadline, now passed. Correction: the previous edition said CVE-2026-20316 had been in KEV since 29 July and was flagged for ransomware use. The KEV catalog has no entry for it; 29 July is when exploitation was first reported. Update, 16 September: Cisco published its September hardening advisory for ASA, FTD and FMC (cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN). It covers eight CVEs found in internal review, CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, with fixed FTD and FMC releases 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0; it went to revision 1.1 on 18 September with an updated ASA fixed-release table. Its statement that two vulnerabilities “belonging to this vulnerability class” are known to be exploited refers to CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316, not to the hardening CVEs, which Cisco does not report as exploited; the full 77-CVE batch has its own card below.
