_threatfeed.date_note: Talos report 9 Sep 2026; hardening advisory 16 Sep 2026, revised 18 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA added three Linux kernel flaws to KEV with a three-day deadline — nobody has said how they are being exploited, which is a reason to move faster, not slower
items.content_text: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 18 September with a federal deadline of 21 September, which has now passed. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path, where a zero-length record gets past record-type handling. The Hacker News gives it CVSS 9.8, and Red Hat cites known public exploits. CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in ebtables SNAT handling that leads to privilege escalation, rated CVSS 8.8. CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, rated CVSS 7.8. Red Hat has updated its advisories to acknowledge exploitation, but nobody has said who is exploiting the flaws, how, or whether they are being used together. As of 22 September that is still the case. Related but distinct: on 18 September a researcher published working local-root exploits for four other kernel flaws, CVE-2026-80844, CVE-2026-81000, CVE-2026-68121 and CVE-2026-74469, fixed in current stable and long-term kernels, according to The Hacker News. Those are proof-of-concept releases, not KEV entries, and do not overlap with the trio; keep the two sets apart when you brief. CISA’s entries carry two notes worth reading closely: affected products may be end-of-life, and the vulnerable component can be embedded in other products. The second note is where most enterprises are exposed. General-purpose servers get kernel updates through the normal distribution channel, but appliances, network devices, hypervisor hosts and container platforms built on Linux often do not. Local privilege escalation also matters most on shared systems. On a container node, a CI runner or a multi-tenant server, anyone who can run code there counts as a local user.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; Red Hat; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV-listed 18 Sep 2026; reported 19 Sep 2026; deadline passed 21 Sep 2026

items.title: GitLab’s CVSS 10.0 path traversal reads any file on the server in one unauthenticated request — and went from disclosure to confirmed exploitation in three days
items.content_text: CVE-2026-85706 is an unauthenticated path traversal in the repository commits interface of self-managed GitLab: a single crafted HTTP request returns the contents of an arbitrary file from the server, with no credentials and no user interaction. GitLab disclosed and patched it on 10–11 September (its patch-release feed dates the release 10 September) in 19.3.2, 19.2.6 and 19.1.8, a release that also fixed CVE-2026-87719, a critical insecure-deserialisation flaw in the Enterprise Edition’s GraphQL subscription handling; no further GitLab patch release had appeared by 22 September. Affected versions run from 18.7 through 19.1.8, 19.2 through 19.2.6 and 19.3 through 19.3.2, and the instance needs at least one public project for the request to land. watchTowr Labs and CISA both reported internet-wide probing almost immediately, and on 14 September CISA and GitLab each confirmed exploitation in the wild; the flaw was added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 September with a federal civilian deadline of 14 September, now passed. On 16 September Hong Kong’s HKCERT also warned that the flaw is being exploited in the wild; no count of compromised instances has been published. GitLab.com SaaS customers were not affected. The reason this is worse than a file-read sounds is what a GitLab server keeps on disk. CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens, deploy keys, integration secrets and database credentials all live there, so an arbitrary read is a credential harvest against every pipeline the instance runs — and those credentials keep working after the patch is applied.

_threatfeed.source_name: GitLab advisory; CISA KEV catalog; watchTowr Labs; HKCERT; BleepingComputer; Cybersecurity Dive; Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Disclosed and patched 10–11 Sep 2026; exploitation confirmed 14 Sep 2026

items.title: A ScreenConnect authorisation flaw is being used to push payloads between connected machines — CISA gave federal agencies three days to patch it
items.content_text: CVE-2026-84869 is a missing-authorisation and improper-privilege-management flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, rated CVSS 9.9 and confirmed exploited. Attackers abuse legitimate remote-support sessions to transfer and execute files without the host confirming the transfer, then use social engineering to get a victim to run a modified ScreenConnect client that detects active sessions and propagates VBScript payloads to the machines on the other end of them. That is the worm-like behaviour in the reporting: not a self-replicating network worm, but spread along established trust relationships between a support console and the endpoints it already reaches. Exploitation has been reported since 20 August. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 11 September and, under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, gave federal agencies three days to remediate — an unusually compressed clock that is itself a signal about observed activity. ConnectWise fixed it in version 26.6.5, with disabling the TransferFiles permission offered as an interim mitigation. For anyone whose IT is delivered by a managed service provider, the relevant instance may not be one you administer, and the blast radius runs from that provider outward through every client it supports.

_threatfeed.source_name: ConnectWise advisory; CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV-listed 11 Sep 2026; exploitation reported from 20 Aug 2026

items.title: A crafted email is enough to get root on a Cisco Secure Email Gateway — CVE-2026-76461 is under active exploitation and there is no workaround
items.content_text: Cisco has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in Cisco AsyncOS for Secure Email Gateway, physical and virtual, that lets an unauthenticated remote attacker run arbitrary commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system. Reporting describes the path as SQL injection reached through the appliance’s parsing of an inbound message, which is the uncomfortable part: the attack vector is the product doing its job. No user has to click anything, no management interface has to be exposed, and no credential is needed — the gateway accepts hostile input from the internet by design, and that is the input. All configurations are affected and Cisco states there is no workaround; fixes are in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014, 16.0.4-302 and 16.5.0-780, shipped alongside a security-hardening advisory. Cisco revised the advisory to 1.1 on 17 September to add clarification for clustered appliances; the exploitation statement is unchanged, and the advisory’s own indicator is a search of the mail logs for COPY.*TO PROGRAM. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not affected. Cisco says multiple customers were likely compromised before disclosure and has contacted affected Secure Email Cloud customers with indicators of compromise; attribution is unknown. CISA added the flaw to the KEV catalog on 14 September with a federal deadline of 17 September, now passed. Cisco Identity Services Engine has since followed with an exploited CVSS 10.0 zero-day (see above). That makes three Cisco enterprise products on this page under confirmed exploitation, alongside Secure Firewall Management Center, and all three share a shape: perimeter infrastructure that sees everything, trusted implicitly, and rarely covered by endpoint detection.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT; CISA KEV catalog; SecurityWeek; The Hacker News; BleepingComputer
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory and KEV listing 14 Sep 2026; advisory rev 1.1 17 Sep 2026; FCEB deadline passed 17 Sep 2026

items.title: Orkes Conductor lets an unauthenticated caller submit a workflow whose expressions run unsandboxed — Fortinet reports active attack attempts, and it is not in KEV
items.content_text: Orkes Conductor, the commercial distribution of Netflix’s Conductor workflow-orchestration server, evaluates JavaScript and Python expressions inside workflow definitions using GraalVM evaluators configured with full host access, and versions 3.21.21 up to but not including 3.30.2 accept those definitions from unauthenticated callers. Submitting a workflow with an INLINE, LAMBDA, DO_WHILE or SWITCH task therefore gives operating-system command execution as the Conductor process. The flaw is CVE-2026-58138, rated CVSS 3.1 9.8 and CVSS 4.0 9.3 by VulnCheck as the assigning authority, and was published by NVD on 30 June. FortiGuard’s outbreak alert of 15 September says its telemetry “is observing active attack attempts”; The Hacker News, citing Fortinet, reports 1,290 attempts blocked in 24 hours on 9 September and about 7,000 between 2 and 9 September, with honeypot hits going back to late July. The fix is Conductor 3.30.2 or later, and the immediate mitigation is to take the workflow API off the internet. It was not in the KEV catalog as of the 21 September catalog version, so a KEV-driven patch queue will not have it. Conductor is niche in absolute terms, but the estates that run it, fintech, e-commerce and microservice platforms, tend to give it credentials to everything it orchestrates.

_threatfeed.source_name: FortiGuard outbreak alert; NVD; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Outbreak alert 15 Sep 2026; reported 19 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA now marks the VMware vCenter RCE CVE-2026-59310 as used by ransomware — the flaw that was an espionage story in August is now an extortion one
items.content_text: CISA has updated its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities entry for CVE-2026-59310, a remote code execution flaw in VMware vCenter Server, to record known use in ransomware campaigns, as reported by BleepingComputer on 15 September. Broadcom patched the flaw on 29 July, and CISA added it to the catalog on 18 August with a federal deadline of 21 August. CISA has not named the ransomware groups involved or said how many organisations are affected. The earlier phase of exploitation is better documented: during mid-August APT activity, the DFIR firm QUIRSO counted 361 compromised IP addresses across 47 countries, and Shadowserver has tracked around 450 exposed vCenter servers. The change of status matters more than the change of wording. vCenter is the control plane for a virtualised estate, so an operator with code execution there can reach every guest it manages at once — which is exactly the position an encryption-focused crew wants, and exactly why a host that was quietly compromised in August may now be holding a second, less patient visitor.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalog; Broadcom; BleepingComputer; QUIRSO; Shadowserver
_threatfeed.date_note: KEV-listed 18 Aug 2026; ransomware use reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Microsoft has now shipped six emergency fixes for its own September update — KB5129195 restores Remote Desktop Services after the record Patch Tuesday broke it
items.content_text: Microsoft released out-of-band update KB5129195 on 14 September to fix RDP connections dropping after several minutes, sign-in failures and servers hanging at configuration prompts, with Microsoft Management Console and File Explorer also affected. It is the sixth emergency patch the company has shipped off the back of this month’s cumulative update — the 8 September Patch Tuesday, the largest on record at 966 to 974 CVEs, including two actively exploited Windows elevation-of-privilege zero-days, CVE-2026-81963 in the Update Stack and CVE-2026-85880 in ALPC. The operational risk now is not the regression itself but the conclusion people draw from it. Six emergency fixes in a week is a strong argument for waiting, and waiting means leaving unpatched two flaws that are already being used to reach SYSTEM — one of which, the ALPC bug, appears in the GRIMWEDGE espionage chain covered elsewhere on this page. The honest position is that this month’s update is both necessary and unusually disruptive, and the answer is sequencing and a pilot ring rather than deferral.

_threatfeed.source_name: Microsoft; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Out-of-band update released 14 Sep 2026; reported 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Cisco’s September hardening batch: 77 CVEs across ASA, FTD, FMC, ISE and IOS XR from internal review, none exploited — do not confuse them with the three zero-days above
items.content_text: Alongside the exploited ISE zero-day, Cisco published on 16–17 September a set of “hardening release” advisories from internal security reviews, 77 CVEs in all according to The Hacker News: 41 for ISE, 28 for Secure Firewall, plus IOS XR. The ASA, FTD and FMC hardening advisory (cisco-sa-hardening-asaftdfmc-uvpPROhN) covers CVE-2026-20329 through CVE-2026-20336, with scores reported from 9.9 down to 7.5 and no workarounds; it went to revision 1.1 on 18 September to update the ASA fixed-release table, which now lists 9.16.4.103, 9.18.4.94, 9.20.4.49, 9.22.3.26, 9.23.1.47 and 9.24.1.26, with FTD and FMC fixed in 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0. The ISE hardening advisory (cisco-sa-hardening-ise-XU5EwX5T) includes two flaws scored 10.0, CVE-2026-20130 and CVE-2026-20192, and states that ISE 3.0 and earlier must migrate to a supported release. The IOS XR advisory (cisco-sa-hardening-iosxr-qg64NcM) covers CVE-2026-20274 through CVE-2026-20280. Separate critical advisories the same day include an FMC Java deserialisation RCE, CVE-2026-20242, and several ISE remote code execution flaws. One sentence in these advisories has been misread elsewhere: Cisco says that one (ISE) or two (FMC) vulnerabilities “belonging to this vulnerability class” are known to be exploited. Those are CVE-2026-76460 and CVE-2026-20079/20316, which have their own cards; the hardening CVEs themselves carry Cisco’s standard statement that it is not aware of malicious use. The practical problem is capacity. Three exploited Cisco flaws already demand emergency changes on the same appliances, and this batch means the emergency change and the hardening change should be planned as one upgrade to a release that covers both.

_threatfeed.source_name: Cisco PSIRT hardening advisories; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 16–17 Sep 2026; ASA/FTD/FMC advisory revised 18 Sep 2026

items.title: Oracle broke its quarterly cadence with a 673-patch “Critical Security Patch Update” — three unauthenticated CVSS 9.8 flaws in E-Business Suite head the list
items.content_text: Oracle issued an out-of-cycle “Critical Security Patch Update” on 15 September, a month before the scheduled 20 October Critical Patch Update, containing 673 new security patches. Oracle describes the new format as a vehicle for “targeted, high-priority security fixes”. Seven flaws score 9.0 or above and all seven are remotely exploitable without authentication: three in E-Business Suite 12.2.3 through 12.2.15, CVE-2026-83327 in the Applications Framework personalisation component over SOAP, CVE-2026-83452 in Document Management and Collaboration over HTTP and CVE-2026-83462 in the Mobile Application Server terminal service over TCP, each 9.8, and four in Communications Unified Assurance 6.1.1 through 7.0.0 (CVE-2026-44024 and CVE-2026-17544 at 9.8, CVE-2026-71290 and CVE-2026-73194 at 9.1), largely in third-party components. E-Business Suite alone receives 159 patches and Oracle Database 11. Oracle repeats its standard statement that it continues to receive reports of attempts to exploit vulnerabilities for which patches already exist, but identifies no flaw in this release as exploited. The context that makes unauthenticated EBS flaws a priority rather than a routine ticket is last year’s Clop campaign against an EBS zero-day, in which an internet-facing ERP became a data-extortion channel for many organisations. An off-cycle release from a vendor known for its quarterly rhythm is itself a signal about how Oracle rates these.

_threatfeed.source_name: Oracle Critical Security Patch Update advisory
_threatfeed.date_note: Released 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Acronis says its cPanel & WHM backup plugin flaw CVE-2026-87886 has been used in limited, targeted attacks and is now in KEV — a root path on shared hosting servers
items.content_text: Acronis advisory SEC-10986 covers CVE-2026-87886, a Linux local privilege escalation caused by insecure file permissions in the Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM and the corresponding Plesk extension. It is low complexity but requires an authenticated local foothold. Acronis says it has seen exploitation in limited, targeted attacks against cPanel & WHM only, based on a report from a potentially affected customer. Fixes are in cPanel & WHM plugin 1.9.3 HF3 and Plesk extension 1.8.11. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 16 September with a federal deadline of 19 September, now passed. The KEV entry covers both the cPanel & WHM plugin and the Plesk extension, although Acronis has reported exploitation against cPanel & WHM only. The scale is small, and the reason it is on this page is the setting: on a shared hosting server, an authenticated local user is simply a customer, or anyone who has compromised one customer’s site, so a privilege escalation in a backup plugin running on every tenant’s box is a route from one site to all of them.

_threatfeed.source_name: Acronis advisory SEC-10986; CISA KEV catalog; BleepingComputer; Help Net Security
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory reported 15 Sep 2026; KEV-listed 16 Sep 2026

items.title: Attackers are uploading PHP web shells to WooCommerce stores through a lead-capture plugin patched in February — Wordfence has blocked more than 100,000 attempts
items.content_text: Wordfence has blocked more than 100,000 attempts to exploit CVE-2026-27540, an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload flaw in the Wholesale Lead Capture plugin for WooCommerce. The plugin’s AJAX upload handler, wwlc_file_upload_handler, does not validate file types, so an anonymous visitor can upload a PHP web shell. Wordfence rates the flaw CVSS 9.8. The shell.php that attackers drop reports host details and provides an upload form for writing more files. Versions up to 2.0.3.1 are affected. The fix, 2.0.3.2, shipped on 20 February 2026, so every site being hit now has gone seven months without applying it. Activity peaked between 4 and 17 June, with further spikes on 1 July and 30 August. The plugin has only about 6,000 active installations, but they are B2B and wholesale storefronts: sites that take trade-account registrations and payments, where a web shell is a short step from card skimming or customer-data theft. It is not in KEV. The pattern matters more than the plugin. Attackers keep scanning for months-old flaws in niche commerce plugins because small stores patch late.

_threatfeed.source_name: Wordfence; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported 15–16 Sep 2026

items.title: WordPress “Click2Shell”: one click by a logged-in administrator installs an attacker’s theme and runs PHP — fixed in 7.1.1, exploit details now public, no CVE cited
items.content_text: BleepingComputer reported on 21 September on a cross-site request forgery chain in WordPress core 7.1.0 and earlier, found by researcher Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, reported to WordPress on 22 August and written up in technical detail on 21 September. If a logged-in administrator opens a crafted link, the chain forces installation of an arbitrary theme and executes PHP during the Customizer preview, because a theme-preview URL value is interpreted one way by the WordPress.org Themes API and a different, buggy way by JavaScript running in the administrator’s browser. The fix is WordPress 7.1.1. Author and editor roles are not enough; the victim must be an administrator. Setting DISALLOW_FILE_MODS gives partial protection. A public proof of concept now exists; no in-the-wild exploitation had been reported at publication. No CVE identifier is given in the reporting and none is invented here; the WordPress.org release notes should be checked for the identifier and the exact release date before this is entered in a tracker. WordPress runs a large share of corporate marketing sites, and the administrators of those sites are usually in marketing or at an agency, log in from the same browser they read email in, and stay logged in. That is the whole attack. Update, 22 September: WordPress 7.1.2 fixes a separate, unauthenticated flaw, CVE-2026-87902, which is under active exploitation attempts. Sites on 7.1.1 need 7.1.2.

_threatfeed.source_name: BleepingComputer; researcher write-up (pwn.ai)
_threatfeed.date_note: Reported to WordPress 22 Aug 2026; details published 21 Sep 2026

items.title: Three JFrog Artifactory flaws chain from anonymous token to administrator in under five minutes — and researchers put half of internet-reachable instances still at risk
items.content_text: Attackers are chaining CVE-2026-42018, a token-disclosure flaw rated CVSS 7.5 that yields an internal anonymous-user JWT even where anonymous access is disabled, with CVE-2026-42016, an insufficient token-validation issue rated CVSS 8.1 that escalates that token to administrator — in some observed cases in under five minutes — before deploying a custom Rust-based command-and-control backdoor. A third flaw, CVE-2026-82329, is a critical authentication bypass in the same product. Attacks were reported publicly from 11 September; Wiz’s timeline puts exploitation of the first two back to 15 August. CISA added those two to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 September with a federal deadline of 25 September, still open, the same day as the four 22 September KEV additions on this page. JFrog has fixed them in 7.111.21 and later, depending on branch. Researchers estimate that between 49% and 62% of internet-reachable Artifactory instances remain vulnerable to at least one of the three. Update, 17 September: Wiz has documented six malicious Groovy user plugins dropped into $JFROG_HOME/var/etc/artifactory/plugins/. They include command shells, a dumper for decrypted LDAP, Crowd and proxy secrets, token tables and signing material, and a memory-resident Tomcat filter backdoor triggered by an X-Request-Trace header. The plugins survive patching and reload on restart, so upgrading closes the way in but leaves the backdoor in place. The severity is not really the CVSS scores, which are moderate individually; it is the position of the product. An artifact registry is the thing your builds trust without checking, so administrator access to it is administrator access to everything compiled, containerised or deployed from it afterwards.

_threatfeed.source_name: JFrog advisory; CISA KEV catalog; Wiz; BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek
_threatfeed.date_note: Attacks reported 11 Sep 2026; KEV-listed 11 Sep 2026; Wiz persistence update 17 Sep 2026

items.title: Check Point’s management and log servers have an unauthenticated root flaw triggered by an over-long username — no exploitation yet, and LivePatch fixes it
items.content_text: Check Point has disclosed CVE-2026-91843, a stack overflow in the login process of its Quantum Security Management Server, Log Server and Multi-Domain Server. A login request with a very long username gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution as root, and the flaw is rated CVSS 9.8. Self-managed and standalone deployments are affected; Smart-1 Cloud is not. Vulnerable builds include R82.10 at Jumbo Hotfix Take 44 or below, R82 at Take 126 or below, R81.20 at Take 166 or below and R81.10 at Take 190 or below. The Hacker News reports that every R82.20 build is affected and that no protective Jumbo Hotfix was yet available for it. End-of-support R81 and R80.x are also vulnerable. The fix is delivered through LivePatch (sk1000155). There is no indication of exploitation and the flaw is not in KEV; Check Point has published detection guidance and indicators. Censys sees about 3,836 hosts exposing the management service’s identity, which counts product presence, not confirmed-vulnerable systems. A management server holds the policy for every gateway beneath it. This disclosure also followed the Dutch NCSC’s warning that exploitation of Check Point’s VPN flaws was imminent. Update, 22 September: that VPN flaw is now exploited and in KEV, and Check Point disclosed a different exploited management-server flaw, CVE-2026-93616, used in targeted attacks in July. CVE-2026-91843 itself is still not reported as exploited or KEV-listed. Both are on the same servers, so close both in one change window.

_threatfeed.source_name: Check Point advisory; BleepingComputer; The Hacker News; Censys
_threatfeed.date_note: Advisory 16 Sep 2026; reported 17–18 Sep 2026

items.title: Google patched the seventh Chrome zero-day of 2026 — and four separate espionage groups were already running the same exploit kit that uses it
items.content_text: Google released a Chrome update on 9 September fixing CVE-2026-87491, an out-of-bounds write in V8, the browser’s JavaScript and WebAssembly engine, and confirmed the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A crafted HTML page is enough to execute code inside the renderer sandbox. The fixed builds are 153.0.8010.36 and .37. This is the seventh actively exploited Chrome zero-day Google has patched in 2026, and it arrives five days after the sixth, CVE-2026-85046, which is also still worth confirming across your fleet. What makes it more than a routine browser patch is who was already using it: researchers found four distinct nation-state-linked groups, one of them APT31 from 28 August, running the same exploit kit — tracked as BlueMoon — chaining CVE-2026-85046 and CVE-2026-87491 inside a single week. Four unrelated actors converging on one chain that fast points at a shared exploit broker rather than four independent discoveries. Two practical notes decide whether you are actually protected. Chrome applies its update on restart, so a fleet where nobody closes the browser is a fleet that is not patched. And every Chromium-based browser in the estate inherits this: Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and any embedded Electron application ship their own V8 and need their own updates on their own vendor schedules. Update: CISA added CVE-2026-87491 to the KEV catalog on 9 September with a federal deadline of 23 September, now passed. Google has since shipped Chrome 153.0.8010.52 and .53 on 17 September with 16 further fixes, two of them rated Critical (CVE-2026-93374 in the Dawn graphics layer and CVE-2026-93372 in WebGL), with no in-the-wild statement for any of them, so the current build is the target rather than .36.

_threatfeed.date_note: Patched and KEV-listed 9 Sep 2026; BlueMoon research 9 Sep 2026; Chrome 153.0.8010.52/.53 on 17 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA and NIST set concrete numbers for cloud identity tokens and signing keys — one-hour tokens, 90-day key rotation for high-impact systems, and no tokens in logs
items.content_text: CISA and NIST have co-authored NIST IR 8587, guidance on protecting the identity tokens and signing keys that cloud authentication depends on. The recommendations are specific. Access and identity tokens should be valid for at most one hour, and expired tokens should be rejected outright. Signing keys should be rotated every 90 days for high-impact systems and annually for others. They should be kept in hardware-backed or isolated storage, and high-impact systems should do their signing in isolated environments. The audience claim should be mandatory, and tokens should never be written to logs. The report cites the 2020 SAML-forgery supply-chain attack, and the incident in which forged tokens exposed more than 60,000 government emails, as the failures it is designed to prevent. It is voluntary and aimed at federal agencies, cloud providers and cloud buyers, which makes it most useful as a procurement and architecture checklist. It lands in a week when the top story turned on a long-lived, over-privileged API key stored in source code, and identity infrastructure such as Cisco ISE was under attack. Long lifetimes, keys that never rotate and tokens left in logs are common, and each is easy to measure.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA; NIST; Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 15 Sep 2026

items.title: Ireland’s DPC fined Google €403 million over location-data processing — a transparency, fairness and retention case, not a breach, with six months to comply
items.content_text: The Irish Data Protection Commission announced on 21 September a fine of €403 million, about US$462 million, against Google for GDPR breaches in how it processed location data through the Web & App Activity, Location History and location-accuracy settings. The inquiry opened in February 2020 and examined practices between May 2018 and February 2020; the findings concern transparency, fairness and retention rather than any security failure, and the DPC ordered Google to bring the processing into compliance within six months. The DPC said location data “can reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private”. Google has said its practices changed from 2019 and did not otherwise comment. Five outlets agree on the figures; the DPC’s own release was not fetched for this edition. It is the fourth-largest fine the DPC has issued. For an IT and security audience the interest is not the sum but the retention finding: the regulator is penalising how long data was kept and how clearly its collection was explained, six years after the practices ended. Any organisation that collects location, telemetry or behavioural data through a product should be able to state, today, what it keeps and why.

_threatfeed.source_name: The Record; SecurityWeek; BleepingComputer; Infosecurity Magazine; The Hacker News
_threatfeed.date_note: Decision announced 21 Sep 2026

items.title: HHS settles with Ambry Genetics for $700,000 over a 2020 phishing breach — and the findings are about risk analysis, leavers and shared accounts, not the phishing email
items.content_text: The US Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights has settled with Ambry Genetics, a genetic testing laboratory in Aliso Viejo, California, for $700,000 and a two-year corrective action plan. The case dates from January 2020, when a phishing attack compromised an employee email account between 22 and 24 January. It exposed data on 225,370 people, including Social Security or driver’s licence numbers, financial information, diagnoses, lab results, medications and treatment details. OCR’s findings are not about the phishing email itself. They cite the lack of an accurate and thorough risk analysis, the lack of procedures for ending workforce access to electronic health information, and the lack of unique user identification. OCR Director Paula M. Stannard said email phishing “can lead to a breach of PHI and reveal HIPAA Security Rule deficiencies.” HIPAA Journal reports that Ambry also settled the related class action for $12.25 million. The lesson reaches beyond healthcare. Six years after the breach, the regulator is asking about three basic controls: a documented risk analysis, a leaver process and named accounts. Any regulated organisation should be able to show all three on request.

_threatfeed.source_name: HHS Office for Civil Rights; HIPAA Journal
_threatfeed.date_note: Settlement announced 17 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA will stop its weekly vulnerability summary after 28 September and point everyone to KEV — check what quietly depends on the old feed
items.content_text: CISA announced on 17 September that it will stop publishing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin after 28 September 2026. The bulletin is the roundup of newly published CVEs with CVSS scores and patch information. CISA is pointing users to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, alerts and advisories instead. The change follows Binding Operational Directive 26-04, issued in June, which directs federal agencies to prioritise remediation by evidence of exploitation and exposure rather than by CVSS alone, with KEV entries first. For most enterprises the bulletin was not the main feed, because scanners and vendor advisories carry the same data. But it is built into more processes than people realise: weekly patch-review meetings, small-team runbooks, managed-service reports and compliance evidence often cite it by name. The substance of the change is sound, and it matches how this page ranks items: an exploited CVSS 7.8 kernel flaw in KEV deserves faster action than an unexploited 9.8. The job now is to make sure nothing quietly stops working when the feed ends.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA; SecurityWeek; Cybersecurity Dive; Dark Reading
_threatfeed.date_note: Announced 17 Sep 2026; final bulletin 28 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA replaced the CERT/CC-built VINCE with its own VINCE-NT for coordinated vulnerability disclosure — the same week it retired the weekly bulletin, and the same shift to prioritisation
items.content_text: CISA launched VINCE-NT on 17 September, a CISA-managed platform for coordinated vulnerability disclosure that replaces VINCE, the Vulnerability Information and Coordination Environment built by CERT/CC in 2020. CISA says the new platform brings more automated advisory workflows, built-in triage and prioritisation, collaboration tools and a simpler submission interface. Active cases are migrating over the coming weeks; inactive cases stay on the old system. Terminology changes too: “vendors” become suppliers, “products” become components and “researchers” become reporters. Read alongside the retirement of the weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin on the card above, it is the second signal in a week that CISA is concentrating on prioritised, exploitation-driven vulnerability work rather than volume publishing. If your product security team receives coordinated disclosures through CISA, or your researchers submit through it, the case links, contacts and process documents will change.

_threatfeed.source_name: CISA; VINCE-NT FAQ (GitHub); Infosecurity Magazine
_threatfeed.date_note: Launched 17 Sep 2026; reported 18 Sep 2026

items.title: FBI: government-impersonation scams took US$1.6 billion from 61,000 victims in 19 months — the professional-licence variant targets doctors and lawyers, and the immigration variant targets your international staff
items.content_text: The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center issued a public service announcement on 18 September on government-impersonation fraud: about 61,000 complaints between January 2025 and July 2026, with losses above US$1.6 billion, an average of roughly US$26,000 each. Fake criminal-charge threats dominate. Jury-duty variants accounted for about 11 per cent (6,833 complaints, about US$36 million); a professional-licence variant, in which callers tell doctors and lawyers their licence is expiring or has been misused, produced 3,322 complaints and more than US$37 million; and “international targeting”, where callers on video from mock government offices threaten foreign nationals and international students with passport cancellation or deportation, was under 3 per cent of complaints but about US$140 million, roughly a tenth of losses. The FBI’s message is simple: no law-enforcement agency will call and demand payment. The PSA number was not captured for this edition and should be checked on ic3.gov. It is on an enterprise page because the victims are employees and the losses arrive at work: a clinician or associate on the phone with a “licensing board”, an international hire told to move money to avoid deportation, and, in the professional-licence case, a pretext that leads naturally to the victim’s work credentials.

_threatfeed.source_name: FBI IC3 PSA via The Register
_threatfeed.date_note: Published 18 Sep 2026

items.title: One extradition and two sentences in a week: alleged Black Axe leaders sent from South Africa to New Jersey, a Conti developer jailed for four years, and a LockerGoga and Nefilim developer given nearly 13 years in Zurich
items.content_text: Five alleged leaders of the Cape Town cell of Black Axe, Perry Osagiede, Franklyn Edosa Osagiede, Osariemen Eric Clement, Collins Owhofasa Otughwor and Musa Mudashiru, all Nigerian nationals arrested in South Africa in 2021, were extradited to the United States in mid-September and have made their first appearances in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey, CyberScoop reported. They are charged with wire-fraud and money-laundering conspiracy over romance and advance-fee scams against US victims running since at least 2011; FBI Newark and the Secret Service led the case, and no fraud total was given. Oleksii Lytvynenko, 44, a Ukrainian who built a malware loader for the Conti ransomware operation from September 2021, held stolen victim data and kept attacking after Conti’s 2022 shutdown, was sentenced on 11 September to four years in US prison for wire fraud, after arrest in Ireland in 2023, extradition in late 2025 and a guilty plea in June. And on 15 September the Zurich District Court sentenced a 52-year-old Ukrainian developer, held since October 2021, to twelve years and nine months for his role in LockerGoga, MegaCortex and Nefilim attacks, including those on Stadler Rail, Meier Tobler and Crealogix, covering more than 1,800 victims in 71 countries; the court found he was not the leader, the verdict can be appealed, and the alleged leader Volodymyr Tymoshchuk remains at large with a US$11 million US reward. None of this changes your exposure this week. It does show, alongside the NightmareStresser seizure, that the pipeline from arrest to sentence is running, and the Conti case in particular that a developer who never touched a victim network is being held to the loader he wrote.

_threatfeed.source_name: CyberScoop; SecurityWeek; The Register
_threatfeed.date_note: Extradition mid-Sep 2026; Conti sentencing 11 Sep 2026, reported 18 Sep 2026; Swiss verdict 15 Sep 2026
